messages.subject: Hierarchical binomial model
parts:
I have a hierarchical model that I'm struggling to implement in r-inla:

y ~ Binomial(p, n)
p = expit(eta + A)
eta ~ N(mu, sig2)
mu ~ N(mu_0, var = S^2)
sig2 ~ InvGamma(a, b)

What I've come up with so far is below. I'm quite sure that something is wrong here based on comparisons with output from other tools. I think the basic issue is that I'm unsure how to decompose the N(mu, sigma^2) random effect into something that INLA handles since none of the random effect handlers deal with a prior on the mean as well as on the precision. 

I was hoping that the use of a constant group id "const" would achieve something similar.

df <- data.frame(y = y, gid = (1:n_arms), const=rep(1, n_arms))
expr = y ~ 0 + f(
    gid,
    model = "iid",
    hyper = list(prec = list(param = c(a, b)))
) + f(
    const,
    model="iid",
    hyper = list(prec = list(initial=1.0 / S^2, fixed=TRUE))
)
result <- inla(
    expr,
    data=df,
    Ntrials = n,
    family = "binomial",
    offset=mu_0 + A
)

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical binomial model
parts:
I've managed to get something that's a step closer using the rgeneric interface. This is producing the correct Q matrix and thus the correct modes as a function of the hyperparameter as confirmed comparing against plots of the joint density. Something is still amiss though because the resulting hyperparameter posterior is very wrong. I'll update the list if I figure it out.

Relatedly: is there a way to access the joint density computation being done internally by R-INLA so that I confirm that my density calculations match with those of R-INLA? That seems like it would be very helpful for debugging!

Thanks again!

my.model = function(
        cmd = c("graph", "Q", "mu", "initial", "log.norm.const", "log.prior", "quit"),
        theta = NULL)
{
    d = 4
    mu_sig2 = 100.0
    sig2_alpha = 0.0005
    sig2_beta = 0.000005
    envir = parent.env(environment())
    interpret.theta = function () {
        return (list(prec = exp(theta[1L])))
    }
    graph = function(){
        return (Q())
    }
    Q = function() {
        p = interpret.theta()
        sig2 = 1.0 / p$prec
        cov = matrix(mu_sig2, nrow=d, ncol=d) + sig2 * Diagonal(d)
        q = solve(cov)
        return (q)
    }
    mu = function() { return (numeric(0))  }
    log.norm.const = function() { return (numeric(0)) }
    log.prior = function() {
        p = interpret.theta()$prec
        val = dgamma(p, shape=sig2_alpha, rate=sig2_beta, log=TRUE)
        return (val)
    }
    initial = function() {
        ntheta = 1
        return (rep(1, ntheta))
    }
    quit = function() { return (invisible()) }

    if (!length(theta)) {
        theta = initial()
    }

    val = do.call(match.arg(cmd), args = list())

    return (val)
}

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Hierarchical binomial model
parts:
Thanks Håvard!

An update on this problem:
- I managed to get the inla.rgeneric version to work! I just had an error in the definition of the log prior.
- And the inla.rgeneric version matches very closely with non-R-INLA results.
- However, the version with two 'iid' random effects still differs by a mild amount from these other results.
- I've traced that problem down to Q matrices being created internally. It seems that R-INLA includes a large precision (of ~1e6) on the error in the equations setting the linear predictor equal to the sum of the two random effects. For particular values of the hyperparameter, that weight seems to be causing some numerical loss of precision. Here is an example:
[1,] 999999.456295093 . . . -999999.442035881 . . . -999999.442035881 
[2,] . 1000000.39393085 . . . -999999.442035881 . . -999999.442035881 
[3,] . . 1000006.12619225 . . . -999999.442035881 . -999999.442035881 
[4,] . . . 1000006.58334297 . . . -999999.442035881 -999999.442035881 
[5,] . . . . 999999.444860636 . . . 999999.442035881 
[6,] . . . . . 999999.444860636 . . 999999.442035881 
[7,] . . . . . . 999999.444860636 . 999999.442035881 
[8,] . . . . . . . 999999.444860636 999999.442035881
[9,] . . . . . . . . 3999998.778193692

In my case rows/cols 1:4 represent the linear predictor, 5:8 represent the InvGamma-prior term and row/col 9 represents the fixed=TRUE term. At this point, my main problem is solved because I am using the rgeneric model. But, I'm still curious what the reason is for including the linear predictors in the rows/cols of the Q matrix? They could be removed such that the Q matrix in this case is 5x5 rather than 9x9. Instead, R-INLA imposes equality between the linear predictors and the other terms using very large precision values, equivalent to including a very small noise term in the model. I understand that this doesn't influence results in the average case but it seems like it dramatically worsens the matrix conditioning and also unnecessarily makes the matrix larger. It also results in surprising behavior where in a model like "y ~ 0", the mode of the linear predictors is not exactly zero but is instead some small multiple of 1e-7 or 1e-6. 

So, I guess my question is why add this noise term and is there a way to control the magnitude? Thanks so much! Lots to learn!
